title: The Slowest Node Sets the Pace
description: Why a cluster runs at the speed of its worst machine, what an all-reduce actually costs, and the hundredfold gap between the wire and local memory.

lines.text: A cluster of two hundred and fifty six machines. One of them is running about twelve percent slower than the rest. Not broken. Slower.
So the cluster runs about twelve percent slower on one two hundred and fifty sixth of its work.
The cluster runs twelve percent slower. All of it. Every machine, every step, for as long as that one machine is in the job.
That cannot be right. The others are not waiting on it for their own arithmetic.
They are waiting on it for the exchange at the end of every step. And that step happens thousands of times, so the twelve percent applies to the entire run and the entire bill.
Nobody gets paged. Every machine reports healthy. This is the most expensive failure mode in distributed training, and it does not look like a failure at all.
AI Infrastructure, episode four. The network.
The least glamorous episode of the series.
And the one that decides whether adding machines makes anything faster. Here is the question. What has to cross the wire, how often, and what does it cost you when it does?
My position is that this is solved. AWS sells a fast fabric, I buy the instances with it, and the framework handles the rest.
The fabric is genuinely excellent, and that is not the same as the problem being solved. Fast networks change where the cliff is. They do not remove it.

sections.title: The exchange at the end of every step

lines.text: Start with what actually happens at the end of a training step, because everything follows from it.

In data parallel training each machine has a full copy of the model and a different slice of the batch. Each computes its own gradients. Those gradients are all different, and they all have to agree before the next step.
So they average them.
They average them, and the operation has a name. An all-reduce: every machine contributes a value, and every machine ends up with the combined result.
Two properties matter. It moves a quantity of data proportional to the size of the model, not the size of the batch. And it is a barrier. Nobody proceeds until everybody has finished.
And there is the twelve percent.
There is the cold open in one sentence. A barrier converts the slowest participant into the speed of the whole system, thousands of times per run.
Now the fabric itself. AWS uses the Elastic Fabric Adapter, and the important thing about it is not raw bandwidth. It is that it bypasses the operating system.
Meaning the network card talks to memory directly.
Directly, without the kernel in the path for every message. That removes latency and, more importantly, removes jitter, which is what a barrier punishes hardest.
Those instances are then assembled into what AWS calls UltraClusters, connected by a non-blocking, petabit scale network.
Define non-blocking, because it is used loosely.

It means the fabric can carry every machine talking at full rate simultaneously, without an internal link becoming a chokepoint. In an all-reduce, where everyone speaks at once, that property is the whole design.
How is the all-reduce actually organised? Because everyone sending to everyone sounds quadratic and therefore hopeless.

It would be, so nobody does that. The classic arrangement is a ring. Each machine sends only to its neighbour, passing partial sums around the circle, and after two laps everybody has the complete result.
The elegant property is that every machine sends roughly the same amount of data regardless of how many machines there are. The cost per machine does not grow with cluster size.
Then scaling is free after all.
The bytes per machine are constant. The number of hops is not. A ring of a thousand machines takes a thousand hops to go round, and every hop adds latency.

So at large scale you stop using one ring and build a hierarchy: combine within a server first, then between servers, then across racks. Bandwidth is the constraint at small scale, and latency becomes the constraint at large scale.
Here is the scenario. You double the machines and throughput improves by about forty percent instead of a hundred. What went wrong?
Overheads. There is always some loss. I would accept forty percent and buy more machines.
Buy more and the next doubling will give you less than forty. That is the part that matters, and it is worth understanding why rather than treating it as a tax.
Each machine now has half as much data per step, so its arithmetic time roughly halves. Good. But the exchange still moves a full model's worth of gradients.
The compute shrinks and the communication does not.
So the ratio of useful work to overhead gets worse with every machine you add. Eventually you reach a point where an extra machine makes the run slower, and you are paying more for less.
Then what do people actually do? Because clusters clearly do scale to enormous sizes.
Three things. First, increase the batch per machine so there is more arithmetic per exchange. That is the simplest fix and it is bounded by memory, which is the previous episode.

Second, overlap. Gradients for the last layers are ready before the first layers have finished, so you start sending those while still computing the rest. Done well, most of the exchange hides behind arithmetic.
Which only helps if there is arithmetic left to hide behind.
Exactly the limit. Overlap buys you a lot and then abruptly stops buying anything, which is why scaling curves bend rather than slope.
Third, hierarchy. Do the expensive, chatty communication over the fast link inside a server, and only cross the slower network between servers when you must.
That is what AWS is selling with UltraServers. Chips inside one are joined by a dedicated interconnect, so a tensor parallel group placed inside that boundary never touches the general network.
And placement therefore matters as much as the hardware.
Placement is the design. Same hardware, two layouts, and the difference in throughput can be several fold.
There is an obvious fourth option you have not mentioned. Send less.
Send less, and there are two honest ways to do it. Exchange gradients at lower precision, which halves the bytes for a small numerical cost, and is now routine.
Or exchange less often. Let each machine take several steps locally before synchronising, so the barrier happens once every few steps instead of every one.
That must change what the model learns.

It does, and that is the catch. The machines drift apart between synchronisations, so you are no longer training quite the thing you thought you were. It works up to a point and then quietly costs you quality.

Which is why it is the last lever rather than the first. Lower precision on the wire is nearly free. Synchronising less often is a trade against the model itself, and it needs measuring, not assuming.
The quantities, because this is an episode where intuition fails without them.
A Trainium two instance has three point two terabits per second of fabric. An UltraServer of four such instances has twelve point eight terabits per second.
Convert to bytes, because memory is quoted that way. Twelve point eight terabits is about one point six terabytes per second.
And the memory bandwidth inside that same UltraServer was one hundred and eighty five terabytes per second.
So the wire is roughly one hundred and fifteen times slower than local memory. That single ratio is the most useful number in distributed training, and it is why hierarchy exists.

Put it in practical terms. Exchanging one hundred and forty gigabytes of gradients at one point six terabytes per second takes on the order of a tenth of a second, at perfect efficiency you will never reach.
A tenth of a second sounds trivial.

Multiply it. Ten thousand steps is a thousand seconds, which is about seventeen minutes of pure exchange. Do that over a run of many days, on a cluster of hundreds of machines, and it is a serious line on the bill.

The newer generation attacks exactly this. Trainium three UltraServers hold up to one hundred and forty four chips, more than twice the previous generation, joined by a switch fabric that AWS says doubles the interchip bandwidth.
More chips inside the fast boundary.

That is the entire strategy. Every chip you move inside the fast domain is a chip whose chatter never reaches the slow one, and those clusters scale to hundreds of thousands of chips on a non-blocking petabit network.
One pass, nothing new.
Data parallel training ends every step with an all-reduce: everyone contributes gradients, everyone receives the combined result. It moves data proportional to the model, and it is a barrier.
Because it is a barrier, the slowest machine sets the pace for all of them, on every step, for the whole run.

The fabric is the Elastic Fabric Adapter, which bypasses the operating system to cut latency and jitter, assembled into non-blocking UltraClusters. Three point two terabits per instance, twelve point eight per UltraServer.

That is about one point six terabytes per second, against one hundred and eighty five terabytes per second of local memory. Roughly one hundred times slower, which is why placement decides performance.

Scaling stops working because compute per machine shrinks while the exchange does not. You buy headroom with a larger batch per machine, by overlapping communication with computation, and by keeping chatty parallelism inside the fastest interconnect available.
Three failures, and the signal for each.
First, the straggler from the cold open. One machine slightly slower, everything slower. It is not an outage, so nothing alerts.
And the signal?

Per machine step times, compared against each other rather than against a threshold. You are looking for one machine consistently at the top of the distribution. An average hides this perfectly, which is why averages are the wrong tool here.
Second, bad placement. The job lands spread across the data centre rather than packed into adjacent hardware, and the chatty communication crosses more of the network than it should.
The signal is a run that is markedly slower than the same configuration was last week, with no code change. Same job, different placement, different performance.
Third, the scaling cliff. You add machines and throughput barely moves, or falls. That is communication having overtaken computation.
And the response is not more machines.
The response is a bigger batch per machine, better overlap, or a different split. Adding machines to a communication bound job is buying more of the thing that is already the problem.
Three questions for your own system.
One. Do you measure step time per machine, or only on average? If only on average, you cannot see a straggler at all.
Two. Does your chattiest parallelism sit inside the fastest interconnect you are paying for, or does it cross servers?
Three. When you last doubled the cluster, what did throughput actually do? If nobody wrote it down, you do not know where your cliff is.
And if throughput is already bending?
Then the next machine you add costs full price and delivers a fraction. That is the moment to change the shape of the job rather than the size of it.
And the number to remember out of all of this?
One hundred times. The wire is about a hundred times slower than local memory, and every design decision in distributed training is downstream of that one ratio.
The line for this episode: a barrier turns your worst machine into everyone's speed, and no amount of bandwidth fixes a machine that is merely slow rather than broken.
Next time, what happens when that machine does break. Failure at scale, why checkpointing more often is not the obvious win it looks like, and the arithmetic of how long a cluster can stay up at all.
